title: JRC Marine ES
text: This website describes the processing of data for JRC’s Marine Ecosystem Services Provision Environmental Accounting. The fish provisioning dashboard presents the 2008 to 2023 accounts in 2008 euro.

title: STECF Fleet Segment Data
text:
The fish provisioning accounts are built from a single Excel workbook published by the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF). That workbook is 285 MB, which is too large to keep under version control and slow to open on most machines. This page records what the workbook contains, how we extracted the parts we need, and what the extraction is safe to be used for.
The conversion is done once by data/stecf/stecf_to_rds.R. Its two outputs are committed to the repository; the workbook itself is listed in .gitignore and stays on local machines only. Anyone who needs to regenerate the RDS files can download the workbook again and rerun the script.

title: STECF Fleet Segment Data
text:
Are they the same data?
They are different tables that overlap in one variable. FS data reports the gross value of landings for a fleet segment as totlandginc; the landings sheets report the same economic concept as totvallandg, broken down by species and sub-region. The two agree closely without being identical.

value_by_year <- bind_rows(
  fs_data |>
    filter(variable_code == "totlandginc") |>
    summarise(euro = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .by = year) |>
    mutate(source = "FS data"),
  fs_landings |>
    filter(variable_code == "totvallandg") |>
    summarise(euro = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .by = year) |>
    mutate(source = "FS landings")
) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = source, values_from = euro) |>
  mutate(difference_pct = round(100 * (`FS landings` - `FS data`) / `FS data`, 1)) |>
  arrange(year)

value_by_year |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(`FS data`, `FS landings`), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(difference_pct, decimals = 1)

From 2009 to 2023 the two series differ by less than three percent, so the landings sheets are effectively a disaggregation of the same reporting. They are not an exact one, because the two templates are submitted separately by Member States and because confidentiality suppression and clustering apply differently at the two levels of detail. The 2008 and 2024 gaps are larger for the reasons given below.
The practical consequence for the fish provisioning method is a clean division of labour. Live weight in kilograms exists only in the landings sheets, so the biophysical account has to come from there. Income and expenditure exist only in FS data, so the net economic result has to come from there. That is why the routine reads both.

title: Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
text:
This page documents the R routine that turns the Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries (STECF) extraction (Scientific, Technical and Economic Committee for Fisheries, 2024) into the fish provisioning accounts. Fish provisioning is the ecosystem contribution to the growth of aquatic biomass captured in uncultivated production contexts (Haines-Young & Potschin, 2018), and it is valued here with the resource rent approach of the SEEA Central Framework (United Nations et al., 2014). The companion page on methods states the equations; this page restates the earlier working script in a compact, reproducible form so that the team can inspect each step, reproduce it from the repository alone, and reuse the parts that generalise.
The routine reads two committed RDS files produced from the STECF fleet-segment workbook: FS_data_2008-2024.RDS for income and expenditure, and FS_landings_FAO_2008-2024.RDS for landings in kilograms and euro. Kilograms exist only in the landings file; income and expenditure exist only in FS data. The conversion is documented on the STECF Fleet Segment Data page.
The routine has three components, and they run in this order because the second depends on the first:

the economic component, which reduces the STECF economic variables to a single net economic result per fleet segment and year (Eq. 3 of the methods report);
the biophysical component, which cleans the landings table, harmonises fishing sub-regions, assigns each sub-region to a European sea region, and attaches the species typology;
the resource rent allocation, which distributes each fleet’s net economic result across the sub-regions and species it landed, then fills the gaps left by fleets without usable economic data.







Important2024 is excluded from the valuation



The STECF files run to 2024, but no Member State has reported a usable expenditure series for that year. The latest fully valuable year is 2023. The two year filters below therefore keep year <= reference_year and drop 2024. Landings for 2024 can be shown in physical terms with a provisional caveat; they cannot carry a resource rent.








NoteMonetary values are 2008 euro



Allocation is done in nominal euro. A single step at the end converts resource rent to constant 2008 prices with Eurostat HICP for EU-27 (Eurostat, 2026). The base year is base_year in the parameters chunk; changing it does not touch the allocation. Tables report both nominal and 2008 euro, plus the year-on-year real change in 2008 euro. Physical landings are not deflated.








NotePaths are relative to the project root



_quarto.yml sets execute-dir: project, so every path below resolves from the repository root regardless of where the .qmd file sits. There is no need for here::here() or setwd().




We work in the tidyverse throughout. readxl reads the lookup workbooks, sf joins the results to the marine region geometry, writexl writes the Excel deliverables, and gt formats the inspection tables. The workbooks are written with writexl rather than openxlsx: the latter currently emits drawing relationships with no drawing parts, and Excel refuses to open the file.

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(sf)
library(writexl)
library(gt)

sf_use_s2(FALSE)

Every input and output path is declared once, at the top, so that a reader can see the full data footprint of the routine without scrolling. reference_year is the latest fully valuable year. The two year filters use year <= reference_year rather than year == reference_year; year is already part of every grouping key and every gap-filling join, so the result is a 2008 to 2023 panel with no cross-year contamination.

reference_year <- 2023
base_year <- 2008

# Inputs
stecf_economic_file <- "data/stecf/FS_data_2008-2024.RDS"
stecf_landings_file <- "data/stecf/FS_landings_FAO_2008-2024.RDS"
species_lookup_file <- "data/lookup/3.classification_vs_OFFICIAL.xlsx"
gsa_lookup_file <- "data/lookup/Link_GSA_Marine regions_Mediterranean Sea.xlsx"
hicp_file <- "data/lookup/hicp_eu27.csv"
gis_file <- "data/gisdata/marine_regions.gpkg"

# Outputs
results_dir <- "data/outputs/results"
gis_dir <- "data/outputs/gis"
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(gis_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

title: Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
text:
Sub-region harmonisation
STECF reports fishing areas at a finer resolution than the accounts require, and it mixes two naming systems: FAO fishing areas such as 37.1.1 and General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean sub-areas such as sa21. The table below collapses the finer codes onto the code actually used in the accounts. It reproduces the recodes of the original script exactly.

sub_reg_recodes <- tribble(
  ~from,       ~to,
  "37.1.1",    "sa5",
  "sa21.1",    "sa21",
  "sa21.2",    "sa21",
  "sa21.3",    "sa21",
  "37.2.2",    "sa21",
  "37.1.3",    "sa21",
  "37.3.1",    "sa22",
  "27.2.a.1",  "27.2.a",
  "27.2.a.2",  "27.2.a",
  "27.2.b.1",  "27.2.b",
  "27.2.b.2",  "27.2.b",
  "27.3.a.20", "27.3.a",
  "27.3.a.21", "27.3.a",
  "27.3.c.22", "27.3.c",
  "27.3.b.23", "27.3.b",
  "27.5.a.1",  "27.5.a",
  "27.5.a.2",  "27.5.a",
  "27.5.b.1",  "27.5.b",
  "27.5.b.2",  "27.5.b",
  "27.14.b.1", "27.14.b",
  "27.14.b.2", "27.14.b"

The correspondence between GFCM sub-areas and FAO Mediterranean divisions is held separately in data/lookup. The pipeline does not consume it; it is the reference that justifies the Mediterranean rows of the recode table, and it is the authority against which the sea region rules below can be audited.

gsa_to_fao <- read_excel(gsa_lookup_file, sheet = "Regions division") |>
  rename(sub_reg = `Row Labels`, fao_division = Sea_Region)

title: Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
text:
Sea region assignment
Each harmonised sub-region belongs to one of the four pan-European marine regions of the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, or to the rest of the world when a European fleet lands a catch taken elsewhere. The rules are a direct transcription of the original case_when(); wrapping them in a function means the same classification can be reused by the overuse and blue carbon routines without copying the list of codes again.

neao_sub_regions <- c(
  "27.1.a",  "27.1.b",  "27.10.a", "27.10.b", "27.2.a",  "27.2.b",
  "27.3.a",  "27.3.c",  "27.3.b",  "27.4.a",  "27.4.b",  "27.4.c",
  "27.5.a",  "27.5.b",  "27.6.a",  "27.6.b",  "27.7.a",  "27.7.b",
  "27.7.c",  "27.7.d",  "27.7.e",  "27.7.f",  "27.7.g",  "27.7.h",
  "27.7.j",  "27.7.k",  "27.8.a",  "27.8.b",  "27.8.c",  "27.8.d",
  "27.8.e",  "27.9.a",  "27.9.b",  "27.12.a", "27.12.b", "27.12.c",
  "27.14.a", "27.14.b"
)

assign_sea_region <- function(sub_reg_clean) {
  case_when(
    sub_reg_clean == "0" ~ "unknown",
    sub_reg_clean %in% c("sa28", "sa29", "sa30") ~ "Black Sea",
    sub_reg_clean %in% paste0("sa", 1:27) ~ "Mediterranean Sea",
    str_detect(sub_reg_clean, fixed("27.3.d")) ~ "Baltic Sea",
    str_detect(sub_reg_clean, fixed("27.8")) |
      sub_reg_clean %in% neao_sub_regions ~ "NEAO",
    .default = "ROW"
  )
}

title: Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
text:
Species typology
STECF identifies species by their FAO ASFIS code but says nothing about what kind of animal it is or where in the water column it lives. The methods report fills that gap from FishBase and SeaLifeBase (Froese & Pauly, 2024; Palomares & Pauly, 2024), and the result is the classification workbook already in data/lookup. We derive two attributes from it: species_group, which separates fish from shellfish and from species whose code could not be matched with confidence, and fish_type, the aggregated water column typology of Table 1 of the methods report.

species_types_raw <- read_excel(species_lookup_file, sheet = "Classification")

species_types <- species_types_raw |>
  transmute(
    species_code,
    species_name_lookup = species_name,
    fish_type = Type,
    species_group = case_when(
      fish == 1 ~ "fish",
      shellfish == 1 ~ "shellfish",
      .default = "other"
    )
  ) |>
  distinct(species_code, .keep_all = TRUE)







WarningThis is where the manual Excel merge came from



The original script joined landings to this classification by hand in Excel because the join in R produced double counting. The cause is visible in the workbook: eight species codes appear twice in the Classification sheet, so a plain left_join() duplicates every landing record for those species. distinct(species_code, .keep_all = TRUE) keeps the first entry and removes the duplication, which makes the merge reproducible in R. The check chunk below lists the affected codes so that the team can decide which of the two entries is correct.



species_types_raw |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = species_code) |>
  arrange(species_code) |>
  select(species_code, species_name, Type, fish, shellfish, Other) |>
  gt()

section: Harmonising regions and attaching the typology
text:
Harmonising regions and attaching the typology
Sub-region harmonisation, sea region assignment and the species join all happen in one pipeline. The species join is the step that was previously done by hand in Excel; relationship = "many-to-one" makes dplyr fail loudly if the lookup ever regains duplicate codes, which is the guard the manual workflow lacked.

landings <- landings_raw |>
  harmonise_sub_reg() |>
  mutate(Sea_reg = assign_sea_region(sub_reg_clean)) |>
  left_join(
    species_types,
    by = join_by(species_code),
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  )

Three checks are worth running every time the extraction is refreshed. The first lists species codes present in the landings but absent from the classification workbook; those rows would otherwise reach the accounting tables with a missing fish type. The second compares the species name STECF reports against the name the classification workbook holds for the same code, which is how a mis-assigned code shows itself. The third lists sub-regions that fell through to ROW, the catch-all category and therefore the place where a new or misspelled STECF code will hide.

landings |>
  filter(year == reference_year, is.na(fish_type)) |>
  distinct(species_code, species_name) |>
  arrange(species_code) |>
  gt()

That last check returns two rows. assign_sea_region() matches Mediterranean sub-areas against the literal list sa1 to sa27, so the decimal sub-areas sa11.1 and sa11.2 do not match and fall through to ROW. Both appear in the GFCM correspondence workbook, which suggests they are genuine Mediterranean areas. We have kept the original behaviour rather than silently changing published numbers; the ROW check above shows how much landing is affected, and the team can then decide whether to add the two codes to sub_reg_recodes.

title: Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
text:
Distributing the net result
A fleet earns one net result but fishes several sub-regions and several species, and STECF cannot attribute cost or revenue any more finely than the fleet. The assessment therefore distributes the net result in proportion to the quantities landed, in two nested steps: first across the sub-regions the fleet worked (Eq. 4 and Eq. 5), then across the species it landed in each of those sub-regions (Eq. 6 and Eq. 7).
The original script carried these weights as percentages and divided by one hundred again at each use. We keep them as shares, which is arithmetically identical and removes four opportunities for a misplaced factor of one hundred.

landings_valued <- landings_valued_input |>
  mutate(
    fleet_landed_kg = sum(landed_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(year, fs_name)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    fleet_area_landed_kg = sum(landed_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(year, fs_name, sub_reg_clean)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Eq. 4: share of the fleet's catch taken in this sub-region
    share_fleet_area = fleet_area_landed_kg / fleet_landed_kg,
    # Eq. 5: net result attributable to the fleet in this sub-region
    net_fleet_area = total_net * share_fleet_area,
    # Eq. 6: share of that sub-regional catch made up by this species
    share_species_area = landed_kg / fleet_area_landed_kg,
    # Eq. 7: net result attributable to the species in this sub-region
    net_species = net_fleet_area * share_species_area
  )

title: Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
text:
Observed prices
The accounts report one figure per species, landing country and sub-region, so the fleet dimension is aggregated away here. Dividing the summed net result by the summed quantity gives the implied resource rent per kilogram, which is the price used to value the gap records in the next section.

accounting_keys <- c(
  "year", "country_code", "sub_reg_clean", "Sea_reg",
  "species_code", "species_name", "species_group", "fish_type"
)

rent_prices <- landings_valued |>
  summarise(
    sum_landed = sum(landed_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum_revenue = sum(net_species, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = all_of(accounting_keys)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    price = if_else(sum_landed > 0, sum_revenue / sum_landed, NA_real_),
    price_basis = "observed rent"
  )







NoteTwo deliberate differences from the original script



The original produced this table with mutate() followed by distinct(), which left one row per underlying fleet record rather than one row per accounting key; because the raw sub_reg was among the columns kept, sub-regions that had been collapsed by the recode table survived as separate rows carrying the same group total, and the final aggregation added them together. Using summarise() over an explicit key list produces exactly one row per group and removes that double counting.
The original also guarded the division against a zero in the individual record’s own net value rather than in the group’s total quantity, which set a price to NA for records that had a valid group price. The guard here is on sum_landed, which is the quantity actually in the denominator.

title: Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
text:
Gap set
Landings from fleets without a positive net result are aggregated onto the same accounting keys so that the two halves of the dataset share one grain. They arrive with quantities and no revenue.

price_gaps <- landings_without_rent |>
  summarise(
    sum_landed = sum(landed_kg, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = all_of(accounting_keys)
  )

title: Marine Ecosystem Services Processing
text:
Filling the gaps
Box 2 of the methods report fills the gaps in three passes, each one coarser than the last: the average price of the species in the same country, then in the same sub-region, then across Europe. Each pass keeps what it could value and hands the remainder to the next. Anything still unvalued after the third pass has no observed price anywhere in the dataset for that species.

# Pass 1: average price of the species in the same landing country
filled_country <- fill_price_gaps(
  price_gaps,
  rent_prices,
  by = c("year", "species_code", "species_name", "country_code"),
  basis = "country average"
)

# Pass 2: average price of the species in the same sub-region
filled_sub_reg <- filled_country |>
  filter(price == 0) |>
  fill_price_gaps(
    rent_prices,
    by = c("year", "species_code", "species_name", "sub_reg_clean"),
    basis = "sub-region average"
  )

# Pass 3: average price of the species anywhere in the dataset
filled_europe <- filled_sub_reg |>
  filter(price == 0) |>
  fill_price_gaps(
    rent_prices,
    by = c("year", "species_code", "species_name"),
    basis = "European average"
  )

The passes overlap by construction, so the first two contribute only the records they actually valued. The third contributes everything that reaches it, including the records it could not value; those carry a quantity and a revenue of zero, which is what keeps the physical account complete even where the economic data does not reach. They are also extracted on their own, because their size is a useful measure of that reach.

accounting_records <- bind_rows(
  rent_prices,
  filled_country |> filter(price > 0),
  filled_sub_reg |> filter(price > 0),
  filled_europe |> mutate(price_basis = replace_na(price_basis, "unvalued"))
)

unvalued_records <- filled_europe |>
  filter(price == 0)
